If $s$ denotes its parameter and $T_i=dx/ds$ on the $i$th segment, an ideal clock carried along it records the increment

$$\Delta\tau=\frac1c\sum_{i=1}^k\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}\sqrt{-g(T_i,T_i)}\,ds.$$

The increment is independent of the admissible finite partition, by additivity of the integral, and is additive across corners. On each smooth segment this is the proper-time parameter with $d\tau=c^{-1}\sqrt{-g(dx/ds,dx/ds)}\,ds$. The flat-spacetime specialization is inherited from [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]; extending that convention to the curved prescribed background is a separate adoption of this framework.

When the parameter $s$ is measured in seconds, $x^0=ct$ is in metres, $c$ is in metres per second, and $\tau$ is in seconds. This is a model postulate, not a theorem or a reported measurement. It does not assert that a physical clock realizes the idealization exactly, that the background solves gravitational field equations, or that the test body affects the background.

Let an extended static spherical charged body have radius $\ell>0$ metres, total charge $q\in\mathbb R$ coulombs, and finite total rest energy $Mc^2$ with $M>0$ kilograms. Use the flat-body moment convention of [[def-rpm-body-moments]] in a momentum-rest inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], with $p=Mc\,e_0$ and $o$ the stipulated center of the spherical body. Its rest spatial chart has coordinates $\mathbf x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$; define $r:=|\mathbf x|:=\sqrt{(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2}$, $\widehat{\mathbf r}:=\mathbf x/r$ for $r>0$, and $\overline B_\ell(0):=\{\mathbf x:r\le\ell\}$. The body support lies in $\overline B_\ell(0)$, and $\ell$ is the radius of the specified exterior region. Use the SI constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], including $c$ in metres per second and $\varepsilon_0>0$. On the open exterior spatial region $\Omega_\ell:=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:r>\ell\}$, the static field is assumed to obey
$$\mathbf E(\mathbf x)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\widehat{\mathbf r},\qquad \mathbf B=0.$$
Let $u(\mathbf x)$ be the time-independent vacuum energy density of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] on this exterior region and define $E_{\rm ext}:=\int_{\Omega_\ell}u(\mathbf x)\,d^3x$. Assume the total rest energy is the sum of this exterior field energy and a remaining material-plus-interior contribution $E_{\rm rem}\ge0$. Then
$$Mc^2\ge\frac{q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0\ell},\qquad \ell\ge\frac{q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0Mc^2}.$$
The exact Coulomb exterior and nonnegative energy accounting are hypotheses. The theorem does not infer an exterior field from spherical symmetry alone. No identification of field energy with an ideal point particle's rest mass is made.

derivations.claim: In case (a) of [A1], [F1] gives $\ell\ge q^2/(8\pi\varepsilon_0Mc^2)$. The numerator is strictly positive and the denominator is finite positive, so this lower bound is positive and independent of $\ell$; consequently $\ell$ cannot tend to zero under the fixed-$q,M$ assumptions.

In case (b) of [A1], substitute $q=\lambda q_0$, $M=\lambda M_0$, and $\ell=\lambda\ell_0$ into [F1]. Since $\lambda>0$, division by $\lambda$ gives $\ell_0\ge q_0^2/(8\pi\varepsilon_0M_0c^2)$. Thus the necessary size ratio is scale-independent. The argument is only a necessary condition on members that already satisfy the static model; it supplies no construction, stability result, or empirical inference.

Adopt the following motion principle for the massive charged test body of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]. Let $a<b$ be finite real parameters and let $z:[a,b]\to O$ be a $C^2$ future-directed timelike segment in a local potential domain, with its endpoint events fixed in the variations. A change from this parameter interval to another compact interval $[\tilde a,\tilde b]$ is admissible when it is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\phi:[\tilde a,\tilde b]\to[a,b]$ with $\phi'(\lambda)>0$ throughout; the same oriented segment is then represented by $\tilde z=z\circ\phi$. In any chosen representation write $\gamma:[\alpha,\beta]\to O$ and let $\lambda$ denote its parameter; the choice $\lambda=\tau$ is included when the curve is parameterized by proper time as in [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]. Use seconds for the parameter in SI evaluation.

For each such parameterized segment, the physical trajectories of this idealized model are the stationary points of

$$S[\gamma]=-mc\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma') }\,d\lambda+q\int_\alpha^\beta A(\gamma')\,d\lambda,$$

where $A$ is the prescribed $C^2$ external potential, $F=dA$, $m>0$ is constant rest mass, $q$ is constant charge, and $c>0$ is the SI conversion constant. A local fixed-endpoint variation is a $C^2$ family $\gamma_\epsilon:[\alpha,\beta]\to O$, defined for $\epsilon$ near $0$, with $\gamma_0=\gamma$, each $\gamma_\epsilon$ future timelike, and $\gamma_\epsilon(\alpha)=\gamma(\alpha)$ and $\gamma_\epsilon(\beta)=\gamma(\beta)$; the local variation field is supported in a coordinate chart. The segment is stationary when $\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}S[\gamma_\epsilon]\right|_{\epsilon=0}=0$ for every such variation. A reparameterization acts on the whole family by $\gamma_\epsilon\mapsto\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi$. With $\lambda=\tau$ in seconds, coordinates in metres and $A$ in tesla metres, $S$ has units joule seconds. The potential and metric are fixed inputs, independent of the particle path. This is a local action postulate: no global potential is assumed, and a global field equation or global trajectory is not part of the postulate. Reparameterization invariance and its implication for stationarity are proved separately in [[pthm-rpm-external-charge-action-equivalence]].

This model describes a test body: it does not evaluate the body's own field, include self-gravity, or adopt radiation reaction, variable mass or charge, electric dipole forces, or spin-dependent translational forces. The postulate is an adopted model assumption, not a deduction from the electromagnetic field equations or a claim that nature follows this action.

derivations.claim: The polynomial $\chi=b(x^1)^2/2$ is smooth and $d\chi=b x^1dx^1$, so its only nonzero potential component is $A_1=b x^1$. The alternating coordinate derivatives give $F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a=0$: all off-diagonal partial derivatives vanish and the only diagonal derivative cancels itself. Applying [F2] with initial potential zero gives the displayed action difference. It is fixed under the endpoint-preserving variations of [A1], so stationarity is unchanged.

By [A2] and [F3], stationarity is equivalent to $m\nabla_UU=0$. Since $m>0$ and the metric matrix is constant, [F1] gives $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\eta^{ad}(\partial_b\eta_{dc}+\partial_c\eta_{db}-\partial_d\eta_{bc})=0$; thus the equation is $dU^a/d\tau=0$ in the inertial chart. Apply [F5] to each component on the interval to obtain constant $U=U_0$; applying it to $z^a(\tau)-U_0^a\tau$ gives $z(\tau)=X_0+(\tau-\tau_0)U_0$. Conversely a future-timelike proper-time straight curve has $dU/d\tau=0$ and is stationary by the reverse implication of [F3]. No compatible endpoint curve is asserted to exist for arbitrary endpoint events or arbitrary proper-time duration.

By [F4], $P=mU_0$ is constant, and [F2] gives $\pi_{A,1}=mU_1+qb x^1$. Differentiating along the curve from step 2.1 yields $d\pi_{A,1}/d\tau=qb U^1$, with $U_1=U^1$ by [F1]. Hence the canonical component may vary exactly as stated while $qF^\sharp(U)=0$ and $dP/d\tau=0$. The action shift has units joule-seconds and the canonical covector components have momentum units; neither is an empirical measurement.

Adopt the charged-body quantities of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]], the SI field convention of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and the classical BMT law [[post-rpm-bmt-dipole-model]]. For a trajectory stationary under the local action postulate, the translational force equation is supplied by [[pthm-rpm-external-charge-action-equivalence]]. In flat Minkowski spacetime let $m>0$, $q,g_s\in\mathbb R$, $\alpha=q/m$, $G=g_s/2$, and let $U,s$ satisfy
$$D_\tau U=\alpha F^\sharp(U),\qquad D_\tau s=\alpha\left[GF^\sharp(s)-(G-1)\frac{U}{c^2}g(s,F^\sharp(U))\right],\qquad g(U,U)=-c^2,\quad g(U,s)=0.$$
The tensor equation is covariant under proper orthochronous Lorentz transformations of the complete field and worldline data. If $F=0$, then $D_\tau U=0$ and $D_\tau s=0$. For any acceleration $a=D_\tau U$ within the Lorentz-force model, the $G=0$ branch is Fermi–Walker transport on the orthogonal spin subspace:
$$D_\tau s=\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(Ug(a,s)-a g(U,s)\bigr)=\frac{U}{c^2}g(a,s).$$
For the uniform-field branch, choose an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] with $e_0=U/c$ for the stationary trajectory and with the positively oriented orthonormal spatial basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Let $\mathbf E=0$ and let the constant spatial field be $\mathbf B\ne0$; its norm and cross product are those of the frame's positive-definite spatial structure. Then $U=(c,\mathbf0)$ is stationary, $\widehat{\mathbf B}:=\mathbf B/|\mathbf B|$, and for $\mathbf s_0:=\mathbf s(\tau_0)$ define $\mathbf s_{\parallel,0}:=(\mathbf s_0\cdot\widehat{\mathbf B})\widehat{\mathbf B}$ and $\mathbf s_{\perp,0}:=\mathbf s_0-\mathbf s_{\parallel,0}$. The $G$ branch has the exact solution
$$\mathbf s(\tau)=\mathbf s_{\parallel,0}+\cos(\omega\Delta\tau)\mathbf s_{\perp,0}-\sin(\omega\Delta\tau)\widehat{\mathbf B}\times\mathbf s_{\perp,0},\qquad \omega=\frac{qG}{m}|\mathbf B|,\quad \Delta\tau=\tau-\tau_0.$$
The $F=0$, $G=0$, and uniform-field claims are deductions within the adopted model, not experimental statements. For the independent finite-body branch, use the moment and unit convention of [[def-rpm-body-moments]]; the density-to-spin identity below is stipulated data.

Separately, let a flat body have rest momentum $p$, and define $M:=\sqrt{-g(p,p)}/c>0$. Choose its momentum-rest inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] with $e_0=p/(Mc)$ and spatial origin at the stipulated body center. Define $\overline B_\ell(0):=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:|\mathbf x|\le\ell\}$ using the Euclidean norm of its positive-definite spatial rest space. In this frame $p$ has components $(Mc,\mathbf0)$; let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ be its angular-momentum tensor, with $S^{0i}=0$ (hence $S^{ab}p_b=0$), and let $e:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ and $j:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be measurable rest densities, with each component of $j$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^3)$; their units are joules per cubic metre and kilogram per square metre per second, respectively. Assume $e$ and $j$ vanish almost everywhere outside $\overline B_\ell(0)$, $|j|$ is the Euclidean norm and satisfies $|j|\le e/c$ almost everywhere, $\int e\,d^3x=Mc^2$, and the stipulated componentwise spin-density identity
$$\mathbf s_*:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf x\times j(\mathbf x)\,d^3x=\tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}S^{ij}\,\mathbf e_k,$$
where the vector integral is componentwise in the positively oriented spatial basis of this inertial frame.
Then
$$\ell\ge\frac{|\mathbf s_*|}{Mc},\qquad |\boldsymbol\delta|<\frac{|\mathbf s_*|}{Mc}$$
for every observer-induced centroid shift $\boldsymbol\delta$ of the flat SSC translation law; the disk radius is a supremum, not an attained boundary for a timelike observer. These rest-body quantities are Lorentz invariant under transforming the complete body data and its momentum-rest hypersurface. No equality between $\mathbf s$ and $\mathbf s_*$ is assumed, so the size inequalities do not bound the BMT polarization unless such an identification is separately adopted.

coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] for the canonical tangent-bundle and connection suppliers used by the BMT transport and charged-action equivalence. No full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Adopt the charged-body quantities of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]], the SI field convention of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and the classical BMT law [[post-rpm-bmt-dipole-model]]. For a trajectory stationary under the local action postulate, the translational force equation is supplied by [[pthm-rpm-external-charge-action-equivalence]]. In flat Minkowski spacetime let $m>0$, $q,g_s\in\mathbb R$, $\alpha=q/m$, $G=g_s/2$, and let $U,s$ satisfy
$$D_\tau U=\alpha F^\sharp(U),\qquad D_\tau s=\alpha\left[GF^\sharp(s)-(G-1)\frac{U}{c^2}g(s,F^\sharp(U))\right],\qquad g(U,U)=-c^2,\quad g(U,s)=0.$$
The tensor equation is covariant under proper orthochronous Lorentz transformations of the complete field and worldline data. If $F=0$, then $D_\tau U=0$ and $D_\tau s=0$. For any acceleration $a=D_\tau U$ within the Lorentz-force model, the $G=0$ branch is Fermi–Walker transport on the orthogonal spin subspace:
$$D_\tau s=\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(Ug(a,s)-a g(U,s)\bigr)=\frac{U}{c^2}g(a,s).$$
For the uniform-field branch, choose an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] with $e_0=U/c$ for the stationary trajectory and with the positively oriented orthonormal spatial basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Let $\mathbf E=0$ and let the constant spatial field be $\mathbf B\ne0$; its norm and cross product are those of the frame's positive-definite spatial structure. Then $U=(c,\mathbf0)$ is stationary, $\widehat{\mathbf B}:=\mathbf B/|\mathbf B|$, and for $\mathbf s_0:=\mathbf s(\tau_0)$ define $\mathbf s_{\parallel,0}:=(\mathbf s_0\cdot\widehat{\mathbf B})\widehat{\mathbf B}$ and $\mathbf s_{\perp,0}:=\mathbf s_0-\mathbf s_{\parallel,0}$. The $G$ branch has the exact solution
$$\mathbf s(\tau)=\mathbf s_{\parallel,0}+\cos(\omega\Delta\tau)\mathbf s_{\perp,0}-\sin(\omega\Delta\tau)\widehat{\mathbf B}\times\mathbf s_{\perp,0},\qquad \omega=\frac{qG}{m}|\mathbf B|,\quad \Delta\tau=\tau-\tau_0.$$
The $F=0$, $G=0$, and uniform-field claims are deductions within the adopted model, not experimental statements. For the independent finite-body branch, use the moment and unit convention of [[def-rpm-body-moments]]; the density-to-spin identity below is stipulated data.

Separately, let a flat body have rest momentum $p$, and define $M:=\sqrt{-g(p,p)}/c>0$. Choose its momentum-rest inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] with $e_0=p/(Mc)$ and spatial origin at the stipulated body center. Define $\overline B_\ell(0):=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:|\mathbf x|\le\ell\}$ using the Euclidean norm of its positive-definite spatial rest space. In this frame $p$ has components $(Mc,\mathbf0)$; let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ be its angular-momentum tensor, with $S^{0i}=0$ (hence $S^{ab}p_b=0$), and let $e:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ and $j:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be measurable rest densities, with each component of $j$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^3)$; their units are joules per cubic metre and kilogram per square metre per second, respectively. Assume $e$ and $j$ vanish almost everywhere outside $\overline B_\ell(0)$, $|j|$ is the Euclidean norm and satisfies $|j|\le e/c$ almost everywhere, $\int e\,d^3x=Mc^2$, and the stipulated componentwise spin-density identity
$$\mathbf s_*:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf x\times j(\mathbf x)\,d^3x=\tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}S^{ij}\,\mathbf e_k,$$
where the vector integral is componentwise in the positively oriented spatial basis of this inertial frame.
Then
$$\ell\ge\frac{|\mathbf s_*|}{Mc},\qquad |\boldsymbol\delta|<\frac{|\mathbf s_*|}{Mc}$$
for every observer-induced centroid shift $\boldsymbol\delta$ of the flat SSC translation law; the disk radius is a supremum, not an attained boundary for a timelike observer. These rest-body quantities are Lorentz invariant under transforming the complete body data and its momentum-rest hypersurface. No equality between $\mathbf s$ and $\mathbf s_*$ is assumed, so the size inequalities do not bound the BMT polarization unless such an identification is separately adopted.

Fix $c>0$ and a future unit observer $n$ in an affine Minkowski spacetime as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. Identify the positive-definite rest space $n^\perp$ isometrically with $\mathbb R^3$, with its Euclidean norm $|\cdot|$ and Lebesgue measure $d^3x$. Define the closed Euclidean ball by
$$\overline B_\ell(0):=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|\le\ell\}.$$
Let $e:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with $e\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and let $j:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be measurable with each component $j_i\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ for $i=1,2,3$. Thus $j$ is vector-valued integrable and every vector integral below is the componentwise Lebesgue integral. Assume $e$ and $j$ are both zero almost everywhere outside $\overline B_\ell(0)$ for some $\ell>0$, and that $|j(x)|\le e(x)/c$ almost everywhere. Define
$$E_0:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e(x)\,d^3x>0,\qquad M:=E_0/c^2,\qquad \mathbf s_*:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}x\times j(x)\,d^3x.$$
Then $\mathbf s_*$ is absolutely integrable and
$$|\mathbf s_*|\le\ell Mc,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \ell\ge\frac{|\mathbf s_*|}{Mc}.$$
The hypotheses are the full mathematical content of this estimate; it is not a bound for a quantum point particle or for a source whose energy density or momentum density fails them.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space, with signature $(-+++)$, and fix $c>0$. Let $p$ be any future timelike vector and define $M:=\sqrt{-\eta(p,p)}/c>0$. Choose an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] with $e_0=p/(Mc)$, so its ordered orthonormal basis is future and positively oriented and $p$ has components $(Mc,\mathbf 0)$ in this frame. Its positive-definite rest space is $e_0^\perp=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; use $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ for spatial components and the induced right-handed symbol $\epsilon_{ijk}$. Let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ satisfy the momentum supplementary condition $S^{ab}p_b=0$, and set $s_*^k:=\tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}S^{ij}$ in this oriented orthonormal rest-space basis. Every future unit observer has the components
$$n=\gamma\left(e_0+\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{v^i}{c}e_i\right),\qquad \gamma=(1-|\mathbf v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2},\qquad |\mathbf v|<c,$$
by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. For every such observer, define
$$\delta^a:=\frac{S^{ab}n_b}{p\cdot n},\qquad S'^{ab}:=S^{ab}-(\delta^ap^b-\delta^bp^a).$$
Then $p\cdot n\ne0$, $\delta\cdot p=\delta\cdot n=0$, and $S'^{ab}n_b=0$. If the representative point changes by $z\mapsto z+\delta$, the total angular momentum $J=z\wedge p+S$ is unchanged by this stipulated spin-shift rule. In the rest space,
$$\boldsymbol\delta=\frac{\mathbf s_*\times\mathbf v}{Mc^2},$$
If $\mathbf s_*\ne0$, the shifts of all future timelike observers fill the open disk in $\mathbf s_*^\perp$ of radius $|\mathbf s_*|/(Mc)$; the boundary is a supremum and is not attained. If $\mathbf s_*=0$, only the zero shift occurs. This is an exact affine-flat algebraic result.

It is distinct from the potential-dependent covector defined in [[lem-rpm-charge-gauge-boundary]].
- The **spin or polarization vector** is a $C^1$ tangent vector field $s(\tau)\in T_{z(\tau)}M$ constrained by $g(s,U)=0$, so it lies in the positive-definite instantaneous rest space $U^\perp$.

Adopt the Schwarzschild exterior vacuum model datum $(M,g,N)$ of [[pthm-gr-schwarzschild-vacuum-model]] with $m_*>0$, $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$. Let $r_E,r_R>s$ be the emitter and receiver radii of static observers in this model. Let $\Delta t\ne0$ be a common Schwarzschild coordinate-time duration over which ideal clocks on these static worldlines accrue proper-time increments $\Delta\tau_E$ and $\Delta\tau_R$. For the frequency ratio, let $\eta:J\to M$ be a specified smooth, affinely parametrized future-directed null geodesic in the exterior and choose $\lambda_E<\lambda_R$ in $J$ so that $\eta(\lambda_E)$ and $\eta(\lambda_R)$ lie on the static worldlines at radii $r_E$ and $r_R$, respectively. Let $\omega_E$ and $\omega_R$ be the ideal geometric-optics frequencies assigned by the corresponding static observers at these endpoint events, using the model's geometric-optics identification with observer energy. With $n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$ the unit static congruence and $U=cn$ the corresponding four-velocity, the ideal-clock and geometric-optics predictions are

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_R}{\Delta\tau_E}=\frac{\omega_E}{\omega_R}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_R)}{f(r_E)}},\qquad \frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_E)}{f(r_R)}}.$$

The proper four-acceleration magnitude required to remain static at radius $r>s$ is

$$a(r)=\sqrt{g(\nabla_UU,\nabla_UU)}=\frac{c^2s}{2r^2\sqrt{f(r)}}=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r^2\sqrt{1-s/r}}.$$

For any $0\le\rho<1$ and radii satisfying $0<s/r_E,s/r_R\le\rho$, define $x_i=s/r_i$ and write $\log:=L$ for the natural integral logarithm of [[def-integral-logarithm]]. The exact logarithmic ratio has the uniform expansion

$$\log\frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\frac{s}{2}\left(\frac1{r_R}-\frac1{r_E}\right)+R,\qquad |R|\le\frac{x_E^2+x_R^2}{4(1-\rho)}.$$

These are conditional deductions of the idealized model; no measured redshift or acceleration is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$,
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with curvature data as in
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]]. On each spherical-polar
product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ define the local frame field

$$e_{\hat0}:=f^{-1/2}\partial_0,\qquad e_{\hat1}:=f^{1/2}\partial_1,\qquad e_{\hat2}:=r^{-1}\partial_2,\qquad e_{\hat3}:=(r\sin\vartheta)^{-1}\partial_3,$$

and for the curvature tensor define the **frame components**

$$\hat R_{\hat a\hat b\hat c\hat d}:=g\bigl(R(e_{\hat c},e_{\hat d})e_{\hat b},e_{\hat a}\bigr).$$

Then:

**(a) The frame field.** $(e_{\hat0},e_{\hat1},e_{\hat2},e_{\hat3})$ is a
smooth $g$-orthonormal frame (tetrad field) on the chart domain, with
$g(e_{\hat a},e_{\hat b})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{\hat a\hat b}$, and
$e_{\hat0}$ is future-directed timelike; it is a tetrad field in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. It is not a coordinate frame.

**(b) Frame components.** The nonzero frame components, up to the
symmetries $R_{abcd}=-R_{bacd}=-R_{abdc}=R_{cdab}$ of
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]], are

$$\hat R_{\hat0\hat1\hat0\hat1}=\frac{f''}{2},\qquad \hat R_{\hat0\hat2\hat0\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat0\hat3\hat0\hat3}=\frac{f'}{2r},$$

$$\hat R_{\hat1\hat2\hat1\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat1\hat3\hat1\hat3}=-\frac{f'}{2r},\qquad \hat R_{\hat2\hat3\hat2\hat3}=\frac{1-f}{r^2},$$

with $f'=s/r^2$ and $f''=-2s/r^3$; all other frame components vanish.

**(c) Kretschmann scalar.** Define the global smooth scalar field
$K:=R_{abcd}R^{abcd}$, with indices raised by the inverse metric. On the
spherical-polar chart locus its component expression is

$$K=f''^2+\frac{4(f')^2}{r^2}+\frac{4(1-f)^2}{r^4},$$

and for the model function $f=1-s/r$ this is

$$K=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}=\frac{48\,G_N^2m_*^2}{c^4\,r^6}.$$

The scalar identity is first computed on the regular angular locus and holds
on all of $M$ by smoothness and density. Since $r>s$ on $M$, one has
$0<K=12s^2/r^6<12/s^4$ at every point; as $r\downarrow s$ the expression has
the finite boundary value $12/s^4$, and the expression $12s^2/r^6$, read as a
function of $r>0$, grows without bound as $r\downarrow0$.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma computes curvature data of the exterior datum on
$r>s$. The limit $r\downarrow s$ is the boundary value on $M$ of the smooth
expression $12s^2/r^6$; no value of the metric at $r=s$ or at $r=0$ is used
or asserted here, those regions being outside the datum (the regular
continuation across $r=s$ is the separate extension lemma of this page).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with Schwarzschild radius
$s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Let
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times S^2$ carry the product
smooth structure and let $\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}:M_{\mathrm{ext}}\to S^2$ be the
third projection. Its product atlas includes ordinary sphere charts at the
poles ([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]).
Define the **tortoise function**

$$r_*(r):=r+s\log\left|\frac{r}{s}-1\right|,\qquad r>0,\ r\ne s,$$

on each of the two intervals $(0,s)$ and $(s,\infty)$, and define the
**advanced-chart metric** globally on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$ by

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv\otimes dv+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+r^2\,\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In spherical-polar product charts its components are

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\,d\Omega^2,$$

namely $g_{vv}=-f$, $g_{vr}=g_{rv}=1$,
$g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=r^2$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$ and all
other components zero. In another sphere chart the angular block is
$r^2(\gamma_{ij})$. Then:

**(a) Smooth Lorentzian metric.** $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and at every point it is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; hence $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$
is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on all of
$r>0$, including $r=s$.

**(b) Time orientation.** The smooth vector field

$$N_{\mathrm{ext}}:=A(r)\,\partial_v-\partial_r,\qquad A(r):=\frac{f(r)+\sqrt{f(r)^2+4}}{2}>0,$$

satisfies $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},N_{\mathrm{ext}})<0$ everywhere
and $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},\partial_v)<0$ everywhere; hence
$N_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a time orientation of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and on the
region $r>s$ it determines the same future cone as the datum's time
orientation $\partial_v=\partial_0$.

**(c) Isometric embedding of the exterior.** The map
$\Phi:M\to M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, $(x^0,r,\omega)\mapsto(x^0+r_*(r),r,\omega)$
restricts to a diffeomorphism of $M$ onto the open subset $\{r>s\}$ of
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and $\Phi^*g_{\mathrm{ext}}=g$; the exterior datum is
therefore isometric to the region $r>s$ of the extension.

**(d) Vacuum and Kretschmann scalar of the extension.** The
metric-selected connection of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ exists and is unique, its
Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and Einstein tensor vanish identically on
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and its Kretschmann scalar equals

$$R_{abcd}R^{abcd}=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}$$

on all of $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$. In particular the scalar is smooth and finite on
the horizon $r=s$, where it takes the value $12/s^4$.

**(e) The horizon is a null hypersurface.** The level set $\{r=s\}$ is a
smooth null hypersurface of $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$ whose null
generator direction is $\partial_v$; every smooth product-chart frame remains
a basis across $r=s$. In spherical-polar charts
$\det(g_{\mathrm{ext}})=-r^4\sin^2\vartheta$; in an arbitrary sphere chart
the determinant is $-r^4\det(\gamma_{ij})$, which is nonzero.

**(f) Scope.** The extension constructed here is a smooth Lorentzian
manifold containing the exterior isometrically and regular across $r=s$; it
is not claimed to be maximal, and no uniqueness or global structure theorem
is asserted. The region $r\le0$ and the surfaces relevant to the Kruskal
model of this page are outside this statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.

derivations.claim: Alternation gives $g(F^\sharp v,w)=F(w,v)=-F(v,w)=-g(v,F^\sharp w)$, so $F^\sharp$ is $g$-skew. By [F1] and the product rule, $$\frac{d}{d\tau}g(U,s)=g(D_\tau U,s)+g(U,D_\tau s)=\alpha\kappa+\alpha\left(a\,g(U,F^\sharp s)+b\,\frac{g(U,U)}{c^2}\kappa\right).$$ Skew-adjointness gives $g(U,F^\sharp s)=-\kappa$, and $g(U,U)=-c^2$; therefore the derivative equals $\alpha(1-a-b)\kappa$.

In any chart along a compact subinterval, the spin equation is a linear system $\dot s=A(\tau)s$ with continuous coefficients: the connection coefficients, $U$, $F$, and $g$ are continuous on the compact curve image. Its right-hand side is locally Lipschitz in $s$, so [F2] gives local existence and uniqueness. The coefficient norm is bounded on each compact chart subinterval, say by $C$; iterating the integral equation gives $\|s(\tau)\|\le \|s(\tau_0)\|\sum_{n\ge0}(C|\tau-\tau_0|)^n/n!=\|s(\tau_0)\|e^{C|\tau-\tau_0|}$. Hence no finite endpoint blow-up occurs there, and finitely many chart subintervals cover any compact part of $I$; uniqueness patches the solutions across chart overlaps.

If $a+b=1$, step 1.1 makes $g(U,s)$ constant, so its zero initial value remains zero. On this constraint, $$\frac12\frac{d}{d\tau}g(s,s)=g(s,D_\tau s)=\alpha\left(a\,g(s,F^\sharp s)+\frac{b}{c^2}g(s,U)\kappa\right)=0,$$ since $F^\sharp$ is skew and $g(s,U)=0$.

In a rest frame $U=(c,\mathbf 0)$ and $g(U,s)=0$ gives $s=(0,\mathbf s)$. The term proportional to $U$ in the spin equation has zero spatial part, while $F^\sharp(s)^i=F_{ij}s^j=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k s_j=(\mathbf s\times\mathbf B)_i$ by [F3]. Thus the spatial equation is $\dot{\mathbf s}=\alpha a(\mathbf s\times\mathbf B)$. When $\alpha\ne0$, equality with [F4] for all $\mathbf s,\mathbf B$ forces $a=G$ (choose nonparallel $\mathbf s,\mathbf B$); preservation for all $\kappa$ then forces $a+b=1$ by step 1.1, hence $b=1-G$. The equations do not identify $a,b$ when $\alpha=0$.

citations.quote:
1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

derivations.claim: Since $S^{ab}p_b=0$ and $p=(Mc,\mathbf0)$, antisymmetry gives $S^{0i}=0$. The observer decomposition [F2] gives $p\cdot n=-Mc\gamma\ne0$, while $n_an_bS^{ab}=0$ and $p_aS^{ab}=0$ give $\delta\cdot n=\delta\cdot p=0$. The definition $s_*^k=\tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}S^{ij}$ inverts to $S^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}s_*^k$: contracting the right-hand side with $\tfrac12\epsilon_{\ell ij}$ gives $s_*^\ell$ by $\tfrac12\epsilon_{\ell ij}\epsilon_{ijk}=\delta_{\ell k}$.

Contracting the spin-shift rule with $n_b$ yields $$S'^{ab}n_b=S^{ab}n_b-\delta^a(p\cdot n)+p^a(\delta\cdot n)=0,$$ because $\delta^a(p\cdot n)=S^{ab}n_b$ by definition and step 1.1 gives $\delta\cdot n=0$. Also $(z+\delta)\wedge p+S'=z\wedge p+S$, which proves the asserted invariance of $J$.

In rest coordinates, $n_j=\gamma v_j/c$, $p\cdot n=-Mc\gamma$, and step 1.1 gives $S^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}s_*^k$. Therefore $$\delta^i=\frac{\epsilon_{ijk}s_*^k\gamma v_j/c}{-Mc\gamma}=\frac{\epsilon_{ijk}s_*^jv_k}{Mc^2}=\frac{(\mathbf s_*\times\mathbf v)_i}{Mc^2},\qquad \delta^0=0.$$ The second equality uses antisymmetry of $\epsilon_{ijk}$ when interchanging $j,k$.

Expanding the coordinate definition [F3] gives $|u\times v|^2=\sum_{i<j}(u_iv_j-u_jv_i)^2=|u|^2|v|^2-(u\cdot v)^2$ and $u\times(v\times w)=v(u\cdot w)-w(u\cdot v)$. Hence $|\boldsymbol\delta|\le|\mathbf s_*||\mathbf v|/(Mc^2)<|\mathbf s_*|/(Mc)$ for $\mathbf s_*\ne0$. Conversely, for any $\boldsymbol\delta\perp\mathbf s_*$ with $|\boldsymbol\delta|<|\mathbf s_*|/(Mc)$, choose $\mathbf v=(Mc^2/|\mathbf s_*|^2)(\boldsymbol\delta\times\mathbf s_*)$. The expanded triple-product identity gives $\mathbf s_*\times\mathbf v=Mc^2\boldsymbol\delta$, and the norm identity gives $|\mathbf v|=Mc^2|\boldsymbol\delta|/|\mathbf s_*|<c$. Thus every interior point occurs; equality in the radius would require $|\mathbf v|=c$, excluded for a timelike observer. When $\mathbf s_*=0$, the formula of step 2.2 gives only $\boldsymbol\delta=0$.

citations.quote: Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold and let $m,c>0$. Let $\mathcal V\subset TM$ be an open set of future timelike vectors and let $f$ be a smooth vector field along the bundle projection $\mathcal V\to M$, with $f(p,V)\in T_pM$ and $g_p(V,f(p,V))=0$ for every $(p,V)\in\mathcal V$. Fix an initial parameter $s_0\in\mathbb R$. For every initial datum $(p_0,U_0)\in\mathcal V$ satisfying $g_{p_0}(U_0,U_0)=-c^2$, there is an open interval $J\ni s_0$ and a unique local solution consisting of a $C^2$ curve $x:J\to M$ and its $C^1$ tangent field $U=dx/ds$, with $x(s_0)=p_0$, $U(s_0)=U_0$, $D_sx=U$, and $D_sU=f(x,U)/m$. The solution depends smoothly on its initial data and on any finite-dimensional parameters on which $f$ depends smoothly, on a common sufficiently short compact interval containing $s_0$ near the base datum. It remains on the future unit timelike shell. There is a unique maximal solution on an open interval containing $s_0$, but this interval need not be all of $\mathbb R$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, with vector-valued functions, their
components $f_i = \pi_i \circ f$, their limits and their continuity as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

1. **Continuity is componentwise.** Let $(X,d_X)$ be a metric space, $A \subseteq X$,
   $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and $a \in A$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ if and
   only if every component $f_i : A \to \mathbb{R}$ $(i<m)$ is continuous at $a$.
2. **Limits are componentwise.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
   point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let
   $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. Then $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$ if and only if
   $\lim_{x\to c} f_i(x) = L_i$ for every $i<m$ ([[def-function-limit]]).
3. **Algebra.** Let $(X,d_X)$, $A$, $a$ be as in clause 1, let
   $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous at $a$ and let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
   Then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ (defined pointwise) are continuous at $a$; the
   real-valued function $x \mapsto \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); and for every norm $N$ on
   $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ the real-valued function $x \mapsto N(f(x))$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

**Where $m \ge 1$ is spent.** The "if" direction of clauses 1 and 2 divides
$\varepsilon$ by $\iota(m)$, which requires $\iota(m) \ne 0$; and clause 3's last
part quotes a bound available only for $m \ge 1$. The "only if" directions hold
for every $m$ but say nothing at $m = 0$, there being no index $i < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

derivations.claim: Since $G$ is continuous and $K$ is compact, $M:=\max_{w\in K}\|G(w)\|_2$ is finite. By [L4], $G\circ z$ is vector-integrable on every compact subinterval. For $b_0\le s<t<b$, [L2] and [L3] give $\|z(t)-z(s)\|_2=\|\int_s^t G(z(r))\,dr\|_2\le\int_s^t\|G(z(r))\|_2\,dr\le M(t-s)$. Thus $z(t)$ is Cauchy as $t\uparrow b$ and has a limit $z_b\in\mathbb R^8$; because $K$ is compact and closed and the tail lies in $K$, $z_b\in K\subset\mathcal D$.

By [L1], the same smooth shell-force system has a local solution $\widetilde z$ through $z(b)=z_b$ at parameter $b$. The old solution extends continuously to $b$ by step 1.1. Taking the limit in its integral equation shows that the extension satisfies $\dot z=G(z)$ up to $b$ with left derivative $G(z_b)$; $\widetilde z$ has the same value and derivative at $b$. Gluing the old curve on $[b_0,b]$ to $\widetilde z$ just after $b$ therefore gives a solution extending beyond $b$, and local uniqueness in [L1] makes this extension agree with the original on overlaps. This contradicts maximality. Applying the same argument to the reversed parameter proves the left-endpoint case.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with its metric-compatible connection $\nabla$, let $c>0$, and let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve parametrized by proper time $\tau$, with $U=D_\tau z$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. Let $F_\tau$ be a continuous alternating two-form along $z$. Define $F^\sharp_\tau$ by
$$g(F^\sharp_\tau(v),w)=F_\tau(w,v).$$
Then $F^\sharp_\tau$ is skew-adjoint with respect to $g$.

For constants $\alpha,a,b\in\mathbb R$, consider the restricted linear transport equations
$$D_\tau U=\alpha F^\sharp(U),\qquad D_\tau s=\alpha\left(aF^\sharp(s)+\frac{b}{c^2}U\,\kappa\right),\qquad \kappa:=g(s,F^\sharp(U)).$$
For every initial $s(\tau_0)$ there is a unique solution on each compact subinterval of $I$. Along any such solution,
$$\frac{d}{d\tau}g(U,s)=\alpha(1-a-b)\kappa.$$
Consequently, the orthogonality constraint $g(U,s)=0$ is preserved when $a+b=1$, and on that constraint $g(s,s)$ is constant. For the coefficient comparison, fix a parameter value $\tau$ and put $n:=U(\tau)/c$. Then $n$ is an observer at $z(\tau)$ and its rest space is the three-dimensional positive-definite subspace $E_\tau:=n^\perp=U(\tau)^\perp$ (the observer and projection conventions are those of [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]] and [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]). Choose an orientation of $E_\tau$ and a positively oriented orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; set $e_0:=n$. Let $P_U(v):=v+g(U,v)U/c^2$, the projection onto $E_\tau$. The rest-space matching condition means the pointwise equality
$$\bigl(P_U(D_\tau s)\bigr)^i=\alpha G\,(\mathbf s\times\mathbf B)_i\qquad(i=1,2,3)$$
for every $\mathbf s,\mathbf B$, when $s(\tau)\in E_\tau$. Thus it compares spatial components of the covariant derivative at the event, not the derivative of components in an unspecified moving tetrad. For $\alpha\ne0$, if the coefficients both preserve $g(U,s)=0$ for every initially orthogonal datum and every allowed alternating field and satisfy this matching condition, then $a=G$ and $b=1-G$. Conversely, these coefficients satisfy both requirements. This uniqueness is only within the displayed two-term ansatz; no uniqueness among all covariant spin-transport laws is asserted. If $\alpha=0$, the rest-space matching condition does not identify $a$ or $b$.

Adopt the following motion principle for the massive charged test body of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]. Let $a<b$ be finite real parameters and let $z:[a,b]\to O$ be a $C^2$ future-directed timelike segment in a local potential domain, with its endpoint events fixed in the variations. A change from this parameter interval to another compact interval $[\tilde a,\tilde b]$ is admissible when it is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\phi:[\tilde a,\tilde b]\to[a,b]$ with $\phi'(\lambda)>0$ throughout; the same oriented segment is then represented by $\tilde z=z\circ\phi$. In any chosen representation write $\gamma:[\alpha,\beta]\to O$ and let $\lambda$ denote its parameter; the choice $\lambda=\tau$ is included when the curve is parameterized by proper time as in [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]. Use seconds for the parameter in SI evaluation.

For each such parameterized segment, the physical trajectories of this idealized model are the stationary points of

$$S[\gamma]=-mc\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma') }\,d\lambda+q\int_\alpha^\beta A(\gamma')\,d\lambda,$$

where $A$ is the prescribed $C^2$ external potential, $F=dA$, $m>0$ is constant rest mass, $q$ is constant charge, and $c>0$ is the SI conversion constant. A reparameterization acts on the whole family by $\gamma_\epsilon\mapsto\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi$. With $\lambda=\tau$ in seconds, coordinates in metres and $A$ in tesla metres, $S$ has units joule seconds. The potential and metric are fixed inputs, independent of the particle path. With the covector convention $A_0=-\phi/c$ and $A_i=\mathbf A_i$, they give $F_{01}=-E_0/c$, $F_{ij}=0$, hence exactly the field in [F1]. Thus the action potential-domain hypothesis [A1] is met, and under the exact assumption [A3], [F2] gives its covariant Lorentz-force equation.

Apply [F3] under [A3] to this field: $\dot p_1=F_0$, $\dot{\mathbf p}_\perp=0$, and $\dot{\mathcal E}=F_0v_1$. Integration with the initial data gives $p_1(t)=p_{01}+F_0t$ and constant $\mathbf p_\perp$. By adopted [A2] and the inertial momentum relations [F4], $\mathcal E^2=m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2$; since $\mathcal E=\gamma mc^2>0$, this is $\mathcal E=c\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2}$, while $\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v$ gives $\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/\mathcal E$. Thus the definitions of $\Pi,\mathcal E,\mathbf v$ in the statement follow. Differentiating the shell identity with $\dot{\mathbf p}=F_0e_1$ gives $2\mathcal E\dot{\mathcal E}=2c^2p_1F_0$, hence $\dot{\mathcal E}=c^2p_1F_0/\mathcal E=F_0v_1$, as required by [F3]. Let $a<b$ be finite real parameters and let $z:[a,b]\to O$ be a $C^2$ future-directed timelike segment in a local potential domain, with its endpoint events fixed in the variations. A change from this parameter interval to another compact interval $[\tilde a,\tilde b]$ is admissible when it is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\phi:[\tilde a,\tilde b]\to[a,b]$ with $\phi'(\lambda)>0$ throughout; the same oriented segment is then represented by $\tilde z=z\circ\phi$. For each such parameterized segment, the physical trajectories of this idealized model are the stationary points of

$$S[\gamma]=-mc\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma') }\,d\lambda+q\int_\alpha^\beta A(\gamma')\,d\lambda,$$

where $A$ is the prescribed $C^2$ external potential, $F=dA$, $m>0$ is constant rest mass, $q$ is constant charge, and $c>0$ is the SI conversion constant. A reparameterization acts on the whole family by $\gamma_\epsilon\mapsto\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi$. This is a local action postulate: no global potential is assumed, and a global field equation or global trajectory is not part of the postulate. Reparameterization invariance and its implication for stationarity are proved separately in [[pthm-rpm-external-charge-action-equivalence]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the

citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the
flat spacetime model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and the SI unit
conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], together with
the framework's idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and ideal light
signals:

**(i) Mass and momentum.** Every massive classical particle of the model
carries a positive constant invariant mass parameter $m>0$ and has
four-momentum $P=mU$, where $U$ is the four-velocity of its future timelike
worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]],
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]); $P$ is a vector of $V$
whose SI unit is kilogram metre per second. The formula is adopted only for
$m>0$; the case $m=0$ is not defined by it and is the separate premise
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. In particular $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$
is a consequence of the four-velocity normalisation, not a separate
assumption.

**(ii) Observer measurement identification.** Relative to a future unit
observer $n$, the model identifies the measured energy of the particle with
$E_n(P)$, its measured spatial momentum with $q_n(P)$, its kinetic energy with
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ and its rest energy with $mc^2$, where $E_n,q_n,T_n$ are
the quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; the
units are the joule, kilogram metre per second and kilogram of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. This clause is a formulation
convention identifying mathematical quantities with the quantities the model
calls measured; it is not a measurement report and no experiment is claimed.

**(iii) Isolated collision balance.** An isolated collision is represented by
a mass-specified on-shell collision datum at an event, with finite nonempty
incoming and outgoing lists of the massive particles of (i) and/or the ideal
massless particles of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]], and with
no external four-momentum transfer or omitted leg. The interaction is
idealized as confined to that event. The sum of the incoming four-momenta equals the sum of the
outgoing four-momenta, in the sense of the collision data of
[[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: the model adopts
$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$ for such an isolated datum. No particular
collision is asserted to occur, and no mechanism, probability, cross section
or amplitude is supplied by this clause.

**(iv) Equation of motion for a stipulated force.** Put
$H_c^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. A stipulated force law is a given
map $F:D\to V$ on a given subset $D\subseteq A\times H_c^+$,
with force components in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$. No regularity
away from the specified worldline is assumed. Along a given $C^2$ massive worldline
$x:I\to A$ with $(x(s),U(s))\in D$ for all $s\in I$, the model's particle
equation is $m\,dU/d\tau=F(x,U)$, with
$dU/d\tau$ the proper-time derivative of
[[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], so that the stipulated $F$
is the four-force of the motion. A particular force law, and the existence,
uniqueness and domain of solutions of the resulting equation, are not adopted
here and belong to a separate model.

Empirical support for these assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the
framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks,
ideal light signals and flat spacetime are inherited and travel to every
consumer of this premise.

Use the massive and null sectors as separately adopted in [[post-rpm-massive-test-particle-action]] and [[post-rpm-null-test-particle-action]]. For a massive body of constant mass $m>0$, its **mechanical four-momentum** is $P=mU$, where $U$ is its future unit tangent with $g(U,U)=-c^2$. In the null sector, the mechanical four-momentum is the separately specified nonzero future-null vector $P$ from the einbein formulation; no null proper time or $P=mU$ is defined.

At an event, for any observer $n$ of [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]], define the spatial momentum and observer energy by

$$q_n(P):=P+g(P,n)n\in n^\perp,\qquad E_n(P):=-c\,g(P,n).$$

The projection identity and positive-definiteness of $n^\perp$ are supplied by [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. With SI units, $P$ has units kg m s$^{-1}$, $q_n$ has the same units, and $E_n$ has units joules. This definition is pointwise and does not assert conservation, positivity, or an energy interpretation for an arbitrary vector field that is not an observer.

Let $a,b\in\mathbb R$ with $a<b$, and let $x:[a,b]\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve on the prescribed background of [[post-rpm-test-clock-and-background]]. Let $H:(-\epsilon_0,\epsilon_0)\times[a,b]\to M$ be a $C^2$ variation, for some $\epsilon_0>0$, such that each $H(\epsilon,\cdot)$ is future timelike, $H(0,s)=x(s)$, and $H(\epsilon,a)=x(a)$ and $H(\epsilon,b)=x(b)$. For a spinless, structureless massive test body of constant primitive mass $m>0$, measured in kilograms, and the SI conversion constant $c>0$ metres per second, adopt the action on this finite segment

$$S_m[x]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(dx/ds,dx/ds)}\,ds=-mc^2\Delta\tau,$$

where $\Delta\tau:=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(dx/ds,dx/ds)}\,ds$ is the ideal-clock increment specified by [[post-rpm-test-clock-and-background]] on this smooth segment. The model's free trajectories are precisely the curves stationary under the fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations just specified; this is the local variation class in [[lem-rpm-length-action-first-variation]]. When $s$ is measured in seconds, $T$ has units metres per second, and the action has units joule-seconds. This is an adopted model premise, not a consequence of the metric or clock postulate. It excludes self-gravity, radiation reaction, spin, finite-size structure, particle creation, and quantum effects; it does not assert empirical adequacy for any particular body.

Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
with spatial base $U=\pi(\Omega)$, compact $K\subseteq U$, spatial potential

([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), let $\varepsilon_*$ and $C_2$ be

$\psi(X):=\varphi(LX)$ for $X\in U_L$.

([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). In the standard coordinates,
$\nabla\psi=(\partial_{X^1}\psi,\partial_{X^2}\psi,\partial_{X^3}\psi)$

$D^2\psi:=D(\nabla\psi)$ for its derivative and
$\|D^2\psi(X)\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|D^2\psi(X)v\|_2$.

  a $C^2$ reparametrization $\gamma_\varepsilon$ by $t=x^0/c$ on
  $[0,T_\varepsilon]$, with $dt/ds\ne0$ in its affine parameter $s$,
  whose length-coordinate components are
  $\gamma_\varepsilon(t)=(ct,x_\varepsilon(t))\in\Omega$, with spatial
  trajectory $x_\varepsilon(t)\in K$ and
  $|\dot x_\varepsilon(t)|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon c$ for every such $t$;
- **(H2)** setting $t(S):=LS/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$,
  $X_\varepsilon(S):=x_\varepsilon(t(S))/L$ and
  $W_\varepsilon(S):=\dot x_\varepsilon(t(S))/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$ for
  $S\in[0,S_*]$, and letting $K'\subseteq U_L$ be a compact convex set

  $(X_*,W_*):[0,S_*]\to\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$ with
  $X_*([0,S_*])\subseteq K'$ and

$$X_*'(S)=W_*(S),\qquad W_*'(S)=-\nabla\psi\bigl(X_*(S)\bigr)\qquad(0\le S\le S_*);$$

- **(H3)** $\|D^2\psi(X)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le K_2$ for every $X\in K'$, where $K_2\ge0$.

Then for every $S\in[0,S_*]$, with
$D(S):=\|X_\varepsilon(S)-X_*(S)\|_2+\|W_\varepsilon(S)-W_*(S)\|_2$,

$$D(S)\le\bigl(D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S_*\bigr)\,e^{(1+K_2)S_*},$$

where $C_3$ depends only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension. Consequently the
following hold.

**(i) Convergence.** If $D(0)\to0$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ along the
family, then $\sup_{0\le S\le S_*}D(S)\to0$.

**(ii) Rate for identical data.** If $D(0)=0$, then
$\sup_{0\le S\le S_*}D(S)\le C_3\varepsilon S_*e^{(1+K_2)S_*}=O(\varepsilon)$.

**(iii) Long coordinate times.** The coordinate-time horizon is
$T_\varepsilon=LS_*/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$, so the fixed scaled interval
$[0,S_*]$ corresponds to coordinate times growing like
$\varepsilon^{-1/2}$; the limit statement is therefore not a large-$t$

$$S_m[x]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(dx/ds,dx/ds)}\,ds=-mc^2\Delta\tau,$$

where $\Delta\tau:=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(dx/ds,dx/ds)}\,ds$ is the ideal-clock increment specified by [[post-rpm-test-clock-and-background]] on this smooth segment. The model's free trajectories are precisely the curves stationary under the fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations just specified; this is the local variation class in [[lem-rpm-length-action-first-variation]]. **Adopted convention.** On a prescribed background $(M,g,N)$ from [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]], let $x:[a,b]\to M$, $a<b$, be a continuous piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike curve in the sense of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]: it has a finite partition $a=s_0<\cdots<s_k=b$, each segment is $C^1$ up to its endpoints with future timelike one-sided tangents there, and the two tangents at a corner need not agree. If $s$ denotes its parameter and $T_i=dx/ds$ on the $i$th segment, an ideal clock carried along it records the increment

$$\Delta\tau=\frac1c\sum_{i=1}^k\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}\sqrt{-g(T_i,T_i)}\,ds.$$

The increment is independent of the admissible finite partition, by additivity of the integral, and is additive across corners. On each smooth segment this is the proper-time parameter with $d\tau=c^{-1}\sqrt{-g(dx/ds,dx/ds)}\,ds$. The flat-spacetime specialization is inherited from [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]; extending that convention to the curved prescribed background is a separate adoption of this framework.

When the parameter $s$ is measured in seconds, $x^0=ct$ is in metres, $c$ is in metres per second, and $\tau$ is in seconds. This is a model postulate, not a theorem or a reported measurement. It does not assert that a physical clock realizes the idealization exactly, that the background solves gravitational field equations, or that the test body affects the background.

A stationary massive path on that segment satisfies $D_\tau U=0$ in proper-time parameter, with $P=mU$ and $m>0$ constant. In the separately adopted null sector of [[post-rpm-null-test-particle-action]], stationarity for the einbein action is likewise defined on a finite segment, using independent fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations of the curve and smooth interior variations of the einbein. Its nonzero future-null branch has momentum $P$ satisfying $D_\lambda P=0$ in an affine parameter $\lambda$ with $dx/d\lambda=P$. These equations hold locally on the interiors of the finite segments; their ODE solutions extend uniquely to maximal solutions on open intervals, with no action integrated over an infinite interval. For any $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$ and $p_0\in M$, an initial vector $U_0\in T_{p_0}M$ that is future timelike and satisfies $g_{p_0}(U_0,U_0)=-c^2$ determines a unique local massive solution with $x(\tau_0)=p_0$, $U(\tau_0)=U_0$, and a unique maximal solution on an open interval containing $\tau_0$. Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data

$\varepsilon_*:=\min\{\varepsilon_0,\,1,\,(128C)^{-1}\}$ the following
hold at every $p\in\Omega$ with $\pi(p)\in K$ and every
$0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$:

$$m\bigl(E(\varepsilon)\bigr)\le4C\varepsilon,\qquad m\bigl(H(\varepsilon)\bigr)\le16C\varepsilon\le\tfrac18,\qquad g(\varepsilon)_{00}\le-\tfrac12 ,$$

so the chart field $\partial_0$ is timelike over the spatial compact $K$;
moreover $\partial_0$ is
a Killing field of $g(\varepsilon)$ on $\Omega$. Here, on a Lorentzian
region without a specified global time orientation, **Killing** means

equation as [[def-gr-killing-field]], applied on each locally time-oriented
neighborhood. No global time orientation of $g(\varepsilon)$ is asserted.

**(b) Inverse-metric expansion and uniform bounds.** There is
$C_1=C_1(C,L)<\infty$ such that at these spacetime points, with
$R^{ab}(\varepsilon):=g^{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta^{ab}+\eta^{ac}E_{cd}(\varepsilon)\eta^{db}$,

$$|R^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le C_1\varepsilon^2,\qquad |g^{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta^{ab}|\le C_1\varepsilon,\qquad |\partial^\alpha g^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_1}{L^{|\alpha|}}\quad(1\le|\alpha|\le2),$$

and

$$|\partial^\alpha R^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_1\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}}\qquad(0\le|\alpha|\le2),$$

where $g^{ab}(\varepsilon)$ are the components of the inverse metric
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]).

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
with spatial base $U=\pi(\Omega)$, compact $K\subseteq U$, spatial potential
$\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\varphi$ and $c>0$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), let $\varepsilon_*$ and $C_2$ be
the threshold and constant of
[[lem-gr-weak-field-christoffel-bounds]], let $S_*>0$ and
$0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$, and put
$T_\varepsilon:=LS_*/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$,
$U_L:=\{X\in\mathbb R^3:LX\in U\}$, and
$\psi(X):=\varphi(LX)$ for $X\in U_L$.

Equip each $\mathbb R^3$ here with the Euclidean inner product
$\langle X,Y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^3X^iY^i$ and norm
$\|X\|_2=\sqrt{\langle X,X\rangle}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). In the standard coordinates,
$\nabla\psi=(\partial_{X^1}\psi,\partial_{X^2}\psi,\partial_{X^3}\psi)$
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); write
$D^2\psi:=D(\nabla\psi)$ for its derivative and
$\|D^2\psi(X)\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|D^2\psi(X)v\|_2$.

  $[0,T_\varepsilon]$, with $dt/ds\ne0$ in its affine parameter $s$,

$$X_*'(S)=W_*(S),\qquad W_*'(S)=-\nabla\psi\bigl(X_*(S)\bigr)\qquad(0\le S\le S_*);$$

Assume countable choice ACω, as in [[def-countable-choice]], for the smooth cotangent-bundle carrier convention used by this page; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $\mathcal D$ be an open subset of the time-dependent tangent bundle $\mathbb R\times TQ$ of a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $Q$, and let $L:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. For fixed $t$, the **fibre derivative** is the map

$$\mathbb F L(t,q,v)=(t,q,p),\qquad p(w)=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=0}L(t,q,v+sw),$$

as in [[def-fibre-derivative-and-legendre-transform-of-a-lagrangian]]. In induced coordinates $p_i=\partial L/\partial v^i$.

The Lagrangian is **regular** at $(t,q,v)$ when the velocity Hessian $(\partial^2L/\partial v^i\partial v^j)$ is invertible there; regularity gives only a local inverse branch. It is **hyperregular on a declared domain** when $\mathbb F L$ is a diffeomorphism from that entire domain onto an open subset of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$.

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. $$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For a $C^2$ future-directed timelike worldline $x:I\to M$ on a prescribed smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian background $(M,g,T)$ of signature $(-+++)$, with $m>0$ a fixed primitive mass in kg and $c>0$ in m/s, and any compact segment $[a,b]\subset I$ with $a<b$, adopt the stationary-action model on that segment

$$S_{m,[a,b]}[x]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(x',x') }\,d\lambda.$$

Here $x$ is $C^2$ on a neighborhood of $[a,b]$ (so its tangent is $C^1$ there), and $\lambda$ is an increasing regular parameter. An admissible variation is a one-parameter family $x_\epsilon(\lambda)$ that is $C^2$ jointly in $(\epsilon,\lambda)$, has fixed endpoint events $x_\epsilon(a)=x(a)$ and $x_\epsilon(b)=x(b)$, and remains future timelike for sufficiently small $|\epsilon|$. The integrand is the proper-time length density, so $S_{m,[a,b]}=-mc^2\int_a^b d\tau$; its dimension is action (J s). The adopted premise concerns this ideal free test body only. It is neither a theorem about all matter nor an empirical report, and supplies no backreaction or completeness claim. The flat ideal-clock specialization agrees with [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]; adopting this action on a curved background remains a separate premise.

On a prescribed background $(M,g,T)$, choose an open parameter interval $I$ and a compact segment $[a,b]\subset I$ with $a<b$.
